name: PureVPN
tagline: Consumer VPN subscription with apps for every platform and thousands of servers across dozens of countries.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Consumer VPN pricing is promo-driven and changes constantly, so any number here would be fiction.

verdictSummary: You can absolutely stand up your own WireGuard server in an afternoon, and for the coffee-shop-wifi threat model it is strictly better: you control the box, there is no third party logging anything, and it costs the price of a small VPS. What you cannot build is the thing people actually buy a VPN for, which is somebody else's IP address in a country you are not in, shared with thousands of strangers. A personal tunnel gives you one static IP that is trivially attributable to you, which is worse than useless for geo-unblocking and anonymity. The server fleet, the peering deals, the residential and streaming-friendly IP ranges, the audited no-logs posture, and the native apps on phones and TVs are the product. Build the tunnel, keep the subscription if you wanted the other thing.
coreLoopDIY: Provisions a WireGuard server on a VPS you rent, generates client configs with QR codes, and routes all your traffic through your own box.
requirements: A VPS from any provider, cheapest tier is fine
A domain or just the VPS IP
SSH access and basic comfort with a Linux shell
WireGuard client app on each device, official ones are free
whatYouLose: IP diversity: one static IP tied to your payment method instead of a rotating pool across 60+ countries
Crowd anonymity: on a shared VPN your traffic blends into thousands of users, on your own box every packet is yours
Streaming and geo-unblocking, since datacenter IP ranges get blocklisted fast and nobody is playing whack-a-mole for you
Native apps with kill switches, split tunneling, and auto-connect on untrusted wifi, on iOS, Android, TV boxes and routers
Third-party no-logs audits and a jurisdiction story, which is the whole compliance pitch
Somebody to keep the server patched, up, and not oversubscribed
moatNotes: A VPN's product is literally a fleet of IP addresses in places you are not, plus the ongoing fight to keep those addresses off blocklists. That is a logistics business wearing a software costume.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the encryption was never the hard part. WireGuard is a few hundred lines and a free client, and your own tunnel handles hostile networks fine. People pay for exit points: an IP in Tokyo, an IP in Berlin, an IP that is not obviously yours, and an app on a phone that reconnects itself without being asked. Renting that fleet and keeping it from getting blocklisted is an operations treadmill nobody wants to run personally, and a self-hosted tunnel actively de-anonymizes you compared to hiding in a shared pool.
notes: The tunnel is an afternoon; the fleet of exit IPs in forty countries is not. The moat is scale infrastructure plus the endless blocklist war, sold as a checkbox.
prompt:
Build me a self-hosted WireGuard VPN so I can tunnel my devices through a VPS I control.

Stack, no debate:
- Target OS: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on a fresh VPS (assume root SSH access).
- WireGuard via the wg-quick tooling, installed from apt. No Docker, no orchestration, no control panel.
- Plain bash scripts plus a tiny Python 3 helper for config and QR generation. Standard library only where possible; qrencode from apt for QR codes.

Deliverables in this folder:
1. install-server.sh: idempotent script that installs wireguard and qrencode, enables net.ipv4.ip_forward and IPv6 forwarding, generates the server keypair into /etc/wireguard/ with 0600 perms, writes /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf listening on the port from .env, sets up nftables masquerade on the default egress interface, and enables wg-quick@wg0 via systemd.
2. add-client.sh NAME: allocates the next free IP in the 10.8.0.0/24 pool, generates a client keypair and preshared key, appends the peer block to wg0.conf, applies it live with wg syncconf (no full restart, no dropped peers), writes clients/NAME.conf, and prints the config as a terminal QR code.
3. remove-client.sh NAME: removes the peer, frees the IP, applies live, deletes the config file.
4. status.sh: wraps wg show with last-handshake and transfer counters in a readable table.
5. .env.example with SERVER_PUBLIC_HOST, WG_PORT, WG_INTERFACE, DNS_SERVERS. Read from .env at runtime; never commit .env; never hardcode keys or hosts.
6. README.md: VPS provisioning steps, the one firewall rule to open (UDP on WG_PORT), how to import configs on iOS, Android, macOS and Windows, and how to verify the tunnel with a curl to an IP echo service.

Explicitly in scope: full-tunnel routing (AllowedIPs 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0), per-client keys with preshared keys, IPv6 support if the VPS has it, a kill-switch note using the client apps' own toggles.

Explicitly out of scope: a web UI, user accounts, billing, multi-region anything, telemetry, log shipping, obfuscation or protocol camouflage against DPI. Do not pretend this hides my identity: put a short section in the README stating plainly that this is one static IP traceable to me, that it is good for hostile wifi and bad for anonymity or geo-unblocking, and that no logs are written by default but the VPS host can see everything.

Idempotency matters: re-running install-server.sh must not clobber existing keys or peers. Fail loudly with a clear message if .env is missing a value.
